raw_comment:
What I notice: 
- A comparative bar chart is presented
- Most brides take their spouse’s last name, but the percentage varies by race.
- White brides do this the most (86%), while Hispanic brides do it the least (60%).
- Black brides are the most likely to hyphenate their names (16%).
What I wonder: 
- Why do Hispanic brides keep their last name more often?
- How do culture and religion influence these choices?
- Would the trend be different in same-sex marriages?
How this relates to me and my community: 
Being part of a Jewish community, taking a spouse’s last name is not just a tradition but an expectation. In many Jewish marriages, women adopt their husband’s surname as part of religious and cultural norms. However, hyphenating last names is pretty common in my community, often to honor both family names and maintain a connection to one’s heritage. However, keeping a maiden name entirely is unheard of, as it may be seen as breaking from tradition.
Catchy headline: "Tying the Knot, Changing the Name?"

raw_comment:
1. I noticed from the graph that most people in these three races to hyphenate their name are the black community. I noticed that white people are most likely to take their spouses' names. I also noticed that only ten percent of white people kept their name.

2. I wonder what was the significance of taking this survey and which community did It take place in. I wonder why Hispanics have the lowest rate of taking their spouse's name. Lastly, I wonder why the rate at which the white and black community keep their name is almost equivalent.

3. This graph relates to my community because at some point almost everyone is going to have to think about getting married and go through these types of questions such as what to do with the last name and how they should go about changing it.

4. Differences in the percentages of brides taking, keeping, or hyphenating their spouses last name among these few communities bring out the cultural influence and differences within these communities giving us important discussion topics regarding diversity and customs. 

5. Diversity and the effects it has on names after marriage.

raw_comment:
Who's keeping their last names? 


I notice that the given graph shows that out of White, Black, and Hispanic brides, the White brides are more likely to change their names to their spouse's with 86% of them changing it.  On the other hand, the majority of Hispanic brides are more likely to keep their last names within the three races: 10% of white women keep theirs, 9% of Black women, and 30% of Hispanics keep theirs.

This relates to me because I am a woman and one day I will have to face this decision.  The majority of people will marry one day and that's when they would have to decide what to do.

raw_comment:
I notice that American women taking their spouses' names is the most common choice, which historically speaking has been the case. Black brides were most likely to hyphenate their names (16%) and Hispanic brides were more likely to keep their name (30%).

I wonder why such the different ethnic groups are more likely to keep their spouses name, their own name, or hyphenate. I am speculating it has something to do with culture and tradition, as mentioned previously, the majority of women take their husband's last name because that is what has usually been done in Western Society. I know that Hispanic surnames are really important meaning - wise, especially in such family-centric cultures, so the carrying on of the familial history through the name could be one contributor of Hispanic women keeping their own name. I would assume the same is true for Black women who want to preserve their family history. 

This relates to me and my community because I will likely get married, and am part of the new generation that will marry. As a non-white person of mixed race, I've definitely thought about hyphenating my own name. I think this trend will increase as more people have interracial marriages. 

"Something Old, Something New, or Something Borrowed"

raw_comment:
I notice that American women change their names to varying degrees: 86% of White brides, 73% of Black brides, 60% of Hispanic brides take their spouse's name. Interestingly, Black brides were most likely to hyphenate their names (16%) and Hispanic brides were more likely to keep their name (30%).

I wonder why such a large number of White brides take their spouse's name. Perhaps tradition dictates this trend. Furthermore, since Hispanic individuals often have more than one middle name, perhaps it is related to the bride's not changing their name. I wonder if fewer women will take their spouse's name in the future, considering how difficult it can be to change legal documents.

This relates to me and my community because my generation will be getting married in the next 15 years. As more couples are of mixed race, these statistics may change. I imagine that the number of brides that take their spouse's names will decrease across all races.

"Getting Hitched: Ditching the Name"

In the website of brides changing their last names, we have noticed similar and different things. The graph is separated into how likely the bride change their last name based on race. The graph shows that white people choose to take the spouse's last name more commonly than Hispanics and black people do. While Hispanics are more likely to keep their last name than both black and white people are. Interestingly, white and Hispanic peoples data add up to 99% while black people’s data add up to 98%. Wondering where the missing percentages are going. We are also left wondering why it’s only those three races and not more. It might show others why some races are most likely to change their last name or keep it. We believe that this information has little impact on ourselves or our community. In conclusion,  we are a little surprised that the difference in brides' likelihood to give up their maiden name varies so much by race.

This graph shows the percentage of Black, White, and Hispanic women who take their husbands' names, do not take them, or hyphenate them. It is interesting to see how the graph accurately displays that.

raw_comment: There are a few trends I notice in the data presented, and I’m interested to know the reasons behind them. Black brides were by far the most likely to hyphenate their names, while Hispanic brides were the most likely to keep their maiden names. Of the white brides that did not take their husbands’ names the majority kept their maiden name, rather than hyphenate. I could speculate this to reflect different cultural norms around marriage. Particularly, you could see the significant minority of white brides keeping their maiden names as representing the population of progressive educated professional white women and the 90% who don’t as those who follow more traditional and Christian social moores, which is a division I’ve noticed in my life and communities.

raw_comment: This graph depicts the percentage of brides changing their last name, either taking their spouse's name, keeping their name, or hyphenating it. The percentages vary based on race. I notice that most women of all races take their spouse's last names. I think this is simply because of tradition. Although a fairly large percentage of Hispanic women kept their last name, this may suggest that this tradition of taking your spouse's last name is not very important to Hispanic culture. I wonder if their are other gender traditions that Hispanic culture does not follow. I notice that out of all women who hyphenate their last name, Black women make up the majority, even though it is only 16 percent. I wonder if as time passes, and as a society progress, fewer women will take their spouse's name. I additionally wonder if white women will be the last to completely switch, if there ever is a complete switch. This affects me and my community as since I am a girl, if I get married, I will have to make the choice on what my last name will be. "To Keep or to Change?"

raw_comment:
I’ve noticed that brides generally take their spouse’s last name, with eighty-six percent of white brides taking their spouse's last name having the highest percentage. Thirty percent of Hispanic brides chose not to change their last name, having the highest percentage of brides who chose not to change it. raw_comment:
This graph depicts the results of a survey that asked 2,740 married women of different races in opposite-sex marriages what they did with their last names after marriage. The researchers focused on women from three ethnic categories: White, Black, and Hispanic. The graph clearly shows that, no matter what ethnic background, the majority of women choose to take their partner's last name. 

 However, out of everyone in the survey,Hispanic women were the  most likely to keep their last name with thirty percent of them keeping their name. In comparison only nine percent of  black women w and  ten percent of white women kept their name. I'm curious if Hispanic women keeping their own names has to do with culture. I'm curious why they didn't broaden this survey to include more cultures, which would provide more information if keeping one last name is a cultural phenomena. This is relevant to my community because all of the married women I know have taken their spouses' names, and when I get married, I intend to do the same. 

Title  Should you keep it or lose it?

raw_comment:
In this graph, I noticed that a majority of women of every race are more likely to take their husband's last name than to keep their own. 86% of White women, 73% of black women, and 60% of Hispanic women. I noticed that Hispanic women are the most likely to keep their maiden name with 30% of Hispanic women not taking their husband's last name. I wonder how much this percentage has changed in the last 20 years as I feel that the public is more open to women keeping their last names. I think it can be seen as empowering for women to keep their maiden name. Especially for women in the medical and law field who work for years to earn a degree, only to have someone else's last name attached to it.  I wonder why it is tradition for women to take the man's last name and with the women's movement still on the rise if it will become more normalized for a man to take their wife's last name. This relates to me and my community because I am a girl and at some point in time I will have to decide whether or not I will take my husband's last name or keep my own. 

Headline: Starting a new chapter, with or without a new last name!

raw_comment:
I notice that it is more of a tradition for White women to take their spouse's name and less of a tradition for Hispanic women to take their spouse's name. 86% of White women take their spouse's name, whereas only 60% of Hispanic women take their spouse's name. In addition to White people and Hispanic people, 73% of Black people take their spouse's name. I also notice that Black women hyphenate their last names more frequently than White women and Hispanic women. I find it interesting that White people take their spouse's name more frequently than Black and Hispanic people. I also find it interesting that in general, more women take their spouse's last name than don't. I wonder why this is. I wonder why it became a tradition for women to take their spouse's last name and why White people partake more in this custom than other races. I also wonder why Black people hyphenate their last names more than other races. This relates to myself and my community as most women I know took their spouse's name after marriage. I do not know any married women who kept their last name or hyphenated their last name. I wonder if as time progresses and society becomes less patriarchal women will stop changing their last names and will be proud to keep their names. 

Name Game!

raw_comment:
1) White brides are more likely to take their spouse’s last name (86%) compared to Black brides (73%) and Hispanic brides (60%). Some brides might also take their spouse’s last name on top of their own, with Black brides having the highest percentage in that area (16% compared to 3% (White) and 9% (Hispanic)). No statistic adds up to 100%, both White and Hispanic add up to 99% and Black adds up to 98%. Hispanic brides are the most likely to keep their last name with the highest percentage, 30% compared to 10% (White) and 9% (Black). 
2) Why is it that white brides choose to take their spouse’s last name more than black brides and Hispanic brides? Could it be a result of minorities trying to break cycles? 3) This relates to me and my community because I know multiple women, of various backgrounds, who have taken the last name of their husbands except for my Hispanic mother. I found it interesting to see such high percentages for this considering taking the last name of a man is a very patriarchal thing. 
4) Say Yes To The Last Name?

Black Women are most likley to hyphen their name. While Latino women are the least likely to take their husbands name. White women are most likely to take their husbands name.

Why are white women most likley to change their name?

White Women More Likely To Take Their Spouse's Name

raw_comment:
This graph shows the results from a survey that asked 2,740 married women in opposite-sex marriages what they do with their last names after marriage. The researchers separated these women into three categories based on their races (White, Black, and Hispanic). It is clear from this graph that the overwhelming majority of women take their spouse's name throughout all three races. However, out of all the races surveyed, Hispanic women were most likely to keep their last name as 30% of them chose to keep it compared to Black women (9%) and White (10%). While this graph only surveyed a tiny percentage of America's 332 million-person population, I think that Hispanic women's commitment to keeping their last name shows the pride that they have in maintaining their heritage, especially as a race that is so often discriminated against. Black women show similar respect for their heritage as 16% of Black women hyphenated their last names compared to 3% of White women and 9% of Hispanic women. This is interesting because I feel like I have never heard a hyphenated last name. I wonder how this graph would change if more people and races were included. For example, Asian women were left out of this graph as mentioned in the commentary. This relates to me because I am a young woman who hopes to get married one day, and eventually, will have to decide what to do with my last name. 
"Name Norms after Marriage"

raw_comment:
The graph depicts the percentage of brides, based on their race, and their decision to change their name last after matrimony. For example, this graph shows that statistically, the majority of white brides, end up taking their spouse’s last name (86%). While a majority of Hispanic brides still take their spouse’s last name (60%), Hispanic brides are the most likely to keep their maiden names at 30% compared to white brides (10%) and Black brides (9%). What I wonder is why this survey was so limited. I understand this was a voluntary survey and only 2,740 American brides responded. Even though it was conducted by the Pew Research Center, a reliable source, it does not accurately represent women across America 68.45 million married women across America. Plus, this graph only pertains to same-sex couples and does not include Asian or Indigenous people. I wonder how much this graph would fluctuate if more people responded and more groups were represented. This relates to my community because as a young woman surrounded by other young women, if we choose to get married, we all have to one day decide the fate of our last names. More and more women feel less pressure to have to change their name to please their husbands and decaying, misogynistic societal standards. It will be interesting to see who leaves their last name, who keeps their last name, and who hyphenates.  

“Married Women: Who Will Have to Change Their Drivers License?”

raw_comment:
1. The most noticeable statistic in the graph is that regardless of race, most brides take their spouses' last names. White brides tend to do this the most, and Hispanic brides tend to do this the least. However, a significant amount of Hispanic brides do keep their own last names.

2. I wonder what may be the reason for so many Hispanic brides to keep their own last names, whether it be a cultural reason or something else. And I also wonder why Black women tend to hyphenate their names more than any other race.

3. This graph is especially interesting to me because my mother is White and my father is Asian, yet my mother didn't take my dad's last name or even hyphenate it. While my mother kept her last name, my last name was the one that got hyphenated. My last name consists of my father's last name and then it's hyphenated to my mother's last name. So I don't even have the same last name as either of my parents, instead I have a union of them. 

4. If I were to retitle this graph, I would title it "What do brides do with their last names?"

raw_comment: This graph depicts the percentage of women who changed their name vs kept or hyphenated their name. In the graph, it can be seen that Hispanic brides are most likely to keep or hyphenate their last name (39%). That is a fairly large percentage of brides that chose to not get rid of their last name. Black brides follow hispanic brides with 25% not getting rid of their last name. White brides are most likely to do away with their last name, with only 13% keeping any part of their original last name. I wonder if it is a cultural phenomena among people of other races to keep their last name? Maybe last names are more valued and respected in other cultures vs caucasian people's culture. Most married women I know choose to take their husband's last name. The majority of them are white. I do have an aunt who is white that opted to keep her last name. I also wonder when these statistics were polled. I would title this graph: "Brides: Where Do You Fall? What is the Value of a Last Name?"

raw_comment:
This chart notes the percentage of women changing their last name in marriage across various racial groups.  White women are the most likely to change their last name to that of their husband's. Black women are most likely to hyphenate their last names, and Hispanic women are extremely likely to keep their last name altogether. 
I wonder why Hispanic women keep their name the most among the racial groups polled for the graph. While only 1 in 10 black or white women keep their name, around 1 in 3 Hispanic women do, which is a huge leap. Maybe it's for a cultural reason? I think that Hispanic families tend to be more close-knit, and many Hispanic people live in intergenerational households. It could be for this reason that Hispanic women want to keep this connection to their family and not take their husbands name.
More and more women are choosing to not take the traditional route of taking the husband's last name. It's interesting to see how this trend is occurring among various groups, especially since there are many women in my life.
HEADLINE: I Do or Don't: Say Yes to the Name

raw_comment: In this graph, it is depicting the percentage of bridges who either took their spouse’s last name, kept their last name, or hyphenated the names for three different ethnicities/races (white, black, and hispanic). I noticed that across all three ethnicities/races, the majority of brides took their spouse’s name, with whites having the highest percentage of 86%. Additionally, I noticed that hispanic brides have the highest percentage of keeping their name with a percentage of 30% whereas white and black brides were less likely to keep their names. Also, black brides had the highest percentage amongst the three categories for hyphenated names at 16%. I wonder if culture and marital traditions play a big role in the differences between brides’ decisions with their last names across the three ethnicities/races. I also wonder what this data would have looked like a few decades ago and if the results would be significantly different from modern times. This relates to my community because I have witnessed all three options for last names occurring with married women, although taking their spouse’s name seems to be the most common, and it is important to recognize potential deeper meanings behind these choices. My headline for this graph would be: “Keeping vs. Changing Last Names - A Simple Concept with a Greater Meaning”.

raw_comment:
What I notice: 
- A comparative bar chart is presented
- Most brides take their spouse’s last name, but the percentage varies by race.
- White brides do this the most (86%), while Hispanic brides do it the least (60%).
- Black brides are the most likely to hyphenate their names (16%).
What I wonder: 
- Why do Hispanic brides keep their last name more often?
- How do culture and religion influence these choices?
- Would the trend be different in same-sex marriages?
How this relates to me and my community: 
Being part of a Jewish community, taking a spouse’s last name is not just a tradition but an expectation. In many Jewish marriages, women adopt their husband’s surname as part of religious and cultural norms. However, hyphenating last names is pretty common in my community, often to honor both family names and maintain a connection to one’s heritage. However, keeping a maiden name entirely is unheard of, as it may be seen as breaking from tradition.
Catchy headline: "Tying the Knot, Changing the Name?"

- The majority of women in opposite-sex marriages in the United States still take their husband's last name, with 79 percent following this tradition.
- Younger, more educated, and politically liberal women are more likely to keep their last name or hyphenate.

- Are there significant regional or cultural variations in last name choices among brides?
- How do societal attitudes and norms regarding gender roles impact the decision-making process regarding last name choices?
- What implications, if any, do these trends have for gender equality and identity within marriage and society at large?

How does this relate to you and your community?

- Individuals and communities may reflect on their own attitudes and practices regarding last name choices in marriage.
- This topic can spark discussions about traditional gender roles, individual identity, and the evolving nature of marriage and family dynamics within different cultural contexts.

raw_comment:
1. The first thing I noticed was that quite a few women decided to take their spouses last name. Not as many Hispanic women took their spouses surname compared to white and black women. Hyphenating names isn’t a popular option. 

2. Is the missing 1-2% women who chose not to participate? Why do so many Hispanic women choose to hyphenate their name? What is the significance of this survey?

3. This relates to my community as many women end up taking their spouses last name. At some point in many people’s lives, they have to wonder what to do with their last name.

4. Differences in the percentages of brides taking, keeping, or hyphenating their spouses last name among these few communities bring out the cultural influence and differences within these communities giving us important discussion topics regarding diversity and customs. 

5. Diversity and the effects it has on names after marriage.

raw_comment:
Who's keeping their last names? 


I notice that the given graph shows that out of White, Black, and Hispanic brides, the White brides are more likely to change their names to their spouse's with 86% of them changing it.  On the other hand, the majority of Hispanic brides are more likely to keep their last names within the three races: 10% of white women keep theirs, 9% of Black women, and 30% of Hispanics keep theirs. 

I wonder why different races have different numbers regarding whether they take or do not take their spouse's last name. Does it have to do with their traditions or what inspires them to choose what to do? 

This relates to me because I am a woman and one day I will have to face this decision.  The majority of people will marry one day and that's when they would have to decide what to do.

raw_comment:
I notice that American women taking their spouses' names is the most common choice, which historically speaking has been the case. Black brides were most likely to hyphenate their names (16%) and Hispanic brides were more likely to keep their name (30%).

I wonder why such the different ethnic groups are more likely to keep their spouses name, their own name, or hyphenate. I am speculating it has something to do with culture and tradition, as mentioned previously, the majority of women take their husband's last name because that is what has usually been done in Western Society. I know that Hispanic surnames are really important meaning - wise, especially in such family-centric cultures, so the carrying on of the familial history through the name could be one contributor of Hispanic women keeping their own name. I would assume the same is true for Black women who want to preserve their family history. 

This relates to me and my community because I will likely get married, and am part of the new generation that will marry. As a non-white person of mixed race, I've definitely thought about hyphenating my own name. I think this trend will increase as more people have interracial marriages. 

"Something Old, Something New, or Something Borrowed"

raw_comment:
I notice that American women change their names to varying degrees: 86% of White brides, 73% of Black brides, 60% of Hispanic brides take their spouse's name. Interestingly, Black brides were most likely to hyphenate their names (16%) and Hispanic brides were more likely to keep their name (30%).

I wonder why such a large number of White brides take their spouse's name. Perhaps tradition dictates this trend. Furthermore, since Hispanic individuals often have more than one middle name, perhaps it is related to the bride's not changing their name. I wonder if fewer women will take their spouse's name in the future, considering how difficult it can be to change legal documents.

This relates to me and my community because my generation will be getting married in the next 15 years. As more couples are of mixed race, these statistics may change. I imagine that the number of brides that take their spouse's names will decrease across all races.

"Getting Hitched: Ditching the Name"

raw_comment:
Major Racial differences between last names	

In the website of brides changing their last names, we have noticed similar and different things. The graph is separated into how likely the bride change their last name based on race. The graph shows that white people choose to take the spouse's last name more commonly than Hispanics and black people do. While Hispanics are more likely to keep their last name than both black and white people are. Interestingly, white and Hispanic peoples data add up to 99% while black people’s data add up to 98%. Wondering where the missing percentages are going. We are also left wondering why it’s only those three races and not more. It might show others why some races are most likely to change their last name or keep it. We believe that this information has little impact on ourselves or our community. In conclusion,  we are a little surprised that the difference in brides' likelihood to give up their maiden name varies so much by race.

raw_comment: There are a few trends I notice in the data presented, and I’m interested to know the reasons behind them. Firstly, the demographic most likely to take their husbands names are white brides, while black and hispanic brides are increasingly less likely to take their husband’s names. raw_comment:
This graph depicts the results of a survey that asked 2,740 married women of different races in opposite-sex marriages what they did with their last names after marriage. The researchers focused on women from three ethnic categories: White, Black, and Hispanic. The graph clearly shows that, no matter what ethnic background, the majority of women choose to take their partner's last name. 

 However, out of everyone in the survey,Hispanic women were the  most likely to keep their last name with thirty percent of them keeping their name. In comparison only nine percent of  black women w and  ten percent of white women kept their name. I'm curious if Hispanic women keeping their own names has to do with culture. I'm curious why they didn't broaden this survey to include more cultures, which would provide more information if keeping one last name is a cultural phenomena. This is relevant to my community because all of the married women I know have taken their spouses' names, and when I get married, I intend to do the same. 

Title  Should you keep it or lose it?

raw_comment:
In this graph, I noticed that a majority of women of every race are more likely to take their husband's last name than to keep their own. 86% of White women, 73% of black women, and 60% of Hispanic women. I noticed that Hispanic women are the most likely to keep their maiden name with 30% of Hispanic women not taking their husband's last name. I wonder how much this percentage has changed in the last 20 years as I feel that the public is more open to women keeping their last names. I think it can be seen as empowering for women to keep their maiden name. Especially for women in the medical and law field who work for years to earn a degree, only to have someone else's last name attached to it.  I wonder why it is tradition for women to take the man's last name and with the women's movement still on the rise if it will become more normalized for a man to take their wife's last name. This relates to me and my community because I am a girl and at some point in time I will have to decide whether or not I will take my husband's last name or keep my own.

raw_comment:
I notice that it is more of a tradition for White women to take their spouse's name and less of a tradition for Hispanic women to take their spouse's name. 86% of White women take their spouse's name, whereas only 60% of Hispanic women take their spouse's name. In addition to White people and Hispanic people, 73% of Black people take their spouse's name. I also notice that Black women hyphenate their last names more frequently than White women and Hispanic women. I find it interesting that White people take their spouse's name more frequently than Black and Hispanic people. I also find it interesting that in general, more women take their spouse's last name than don't. I wonder why this is. I wonder why it became a tradition for women to take their spouse's last name and why White people partake more in this custom than other races. I also wonder why Black people hyphenate their last names more than other races. This relates to myself and my community as most women I know took their spouse's name after marriage. I do not know any married women who kept their last name or hyphenated their last name. I wonder if as time progresses and society becomes less patriarchal women will stop changing their last names and will be proud to keep their names. 

Name Game!

Some brides might also take their spouse’s last name on top of their own, with Black brides having the highest percentage in that area (16% compared to 3% (White) and 9% (Hispanic)). 1. The graph shows that brides taking their spouse's last name is more common than keeping it or hyphenating it. I've also seen that white women are more likely than black and Hispanic women to change their last name. I've also seen that roughly 30% of Hispanics preserve their last name. 3. This connects to my community because, while the majority of my community is Hispanic, many of them change their last name to their spouses, but there are still a significant number of them who keep it, as opposed to white and black women. 
4. Brides Choosing Their Last Name

raw_comment:
This graph shows the results from a survey that asked 2,740 married women in opposite-sex marriages what they do with their last names after marriage. The researchers separated these women into three categories based on their races (White, Black, and Hispanic). It is clear from this graph that the overwhelming majority of women take their spouse's name throughout all three races. However, out of all the races surveyed, Hispanic women were most likely to keep their last name as 30% of them chose to keep it compared to Black women (9%) and White (10%). While this graph only surveyed a tiny percentage of America's 332 million-person population, I think that Hispanic women's commitment to keeping their last name shows the pride that they have in maintaining their heritage, especially as a race that is so often discriminated against. Black women show similar respect for their heritage as 16% of Black women hyphenated their last names compared to 3% of White women and 9% of Hispanic women. This is interesting because I feel like I have never heard a hyphenated last name. I wonder how this graph would change if more people and races were included. For example, Asian women were left out of this graph as mentioned in the commentary. This relates to me because I am a young woman who hopes to get married one day, and eventually, will have to decide what to do with my last name. 
"Name Norms after Marriage"

raw_comment:
The graph depicts the percentage of brides, based on their race, and their decision to change their name last after matrimony. For example, this graph shows that statistically, the majority of white brides, end up taking their spouse’s last name (86%). While a majority of Hispanic brides still take their spouse’s last name (60%), Hispanic brides are the most likely to keep their maiden names at 30% compared to white brides (10%) and Black brides (9%). What I wonder is why this survey was so limited. I understand this was a voluntary survey and only 2,740 American brides responded. Even though it was conducted by the Pew Research Center, a reliable source, it does not accurately represent women across America 68.45 million married women across America. Plus, this graph only pertains to same-sex couples and does not include Asian or Indigenous people. I wonder how much this graph would fluctuate if more people responded and more groups were represented. This relates to my community because as a young woman surrounded by other young women, if we choose to get married, we all have to one day decide the fate of our last names. More and more women feel less pressure to have to change their name to please their husbands and decaying, misogynistic societal standards. It will be interesting to see who leaves their last name, who keeps their last name, and who hyphenates.  

“Married Women: Who Will Have to Change Their Drivers License?”

raw_comment:
1. The most noticeable statistic in the graph is that regardless of race, most brides take their spouses' last names. White brides tend to do this the most, and Hispanic brides tend to do this the least. However, a significant amount of Hispanic brides do keep their own last names.

2. I wonder what may be the reason for so many Hispanic brides to keep their own last names, whether it be a cultural reason or something else. And I also wonder why Black women tend to hyphenate their names more than any other race.

3. This graph is especially interesting to me because my mother is White and my father is Asian, yet my mother didn't take my dad's last name or even hyphenate it. While my mother kept her last name, my last name was the one that got hyphenated. My last name consists of my father's last name and then it's hyphenated to my mother's last name. So I don't even have the same last name as either of my parents, instead I have a union of them. 

4. If I were to retitle this graph, I would title it "What do brides do with their last names?"

raw_comment:
What do you notice?

White brides have the biggest percentages of keeping their last names, black brides are second, and Hispanic brides are third. A large percentage of black brides hyphenate their last names and almost no white birdies hyphenate them. Regardless of race, most women change their last names. Hyphenated names are the least common.

What do you wonder?

I wonder why more Hispanic women don’t change their names. I wonder if any of this matters and if changing or not changing your last names has any benefits or disadvantages.

How does this relate to you and your community?

Most women in my community are very traditional and change their last names. I also plan to change my last name when I get married.

Is it better to keep or to change?

raw_comment: This graph depicts the percentage of women who changed their name vs kept or hyphenated their name. Most married women I know choose to take their husband's last name. The majority of them are white. I do have an aunt who is white that opted to keep her last name. I also wonder when these statistics were polled. I would title this graph: "Brides: Where Do You Fall? What is the Value of a Last Name?"

Overall, White women tend to change their last names more than the women of any other race, with a rate of 86% changing their names and only 10% keeping them. This chart is impactful because it depicts different cultural values by showing the importance of keeping one's last name alive in different ethnic groups. 
Graph name- A Bride's Last Name: The Big Choice

raw_comment: I notice that women are more likely to take their husband's last name rather than keep theirs or hyphenate the two together. I wonder what the decision process is when making the decision to keep or change their name. This relates to me because it is biblical for a woman to bear her husband's last name, just as Christians bear Christ's name. It is a symbol of a woman sacrificing her complete freeness to submit and, for lack of better words, "belong" to her husband. I would title this graph "To Change, or Not to Change" (thanks Shakespeare). I chose this headline because it is intriguing, and that is the primary idea this graph is showcasing: whether or not it is more socially accepted or common to change your last name after marriage.

raw_comment:
This chart notes the percentage of women changing their last name in marriage across various racial groups.  White women are the most likely to change their last name to that of their husband's. Black women are most likely to hyphenate their last names, and Hispanic women are extremely likely to keep their last name altogether. 
I wonder why Hispanic women keep their name the most among the racial groups polled for the graph. While only 1 in 10 black or white women keep their name, around 1 in 3 Hispanic women do, which is a huge leap. Maybe it's for a cultural reason? I think that Hispanic families tend to be more close-knit, and many Hispanic people live in intergenerational households. It could be for this reason that Hispanic women want to keep this connection to their family and not take their husbands name.
More and more women are choosing to not take the traditional route of taking the husband's last name. It's interesting to see how this trend is occurring among various groups, especially since there are many women in my life.
HEADLINE: I Do or Don't: Say Yes to the Name

raw_comment: In this graph, it is depicting the percentage of bridges who either took their spouse’s last name, kept their last name, or hyphenated the names for three different ethnicities/races (white, black, and hispanic). I noticed that across all three ethnicities/races, the majority of brides took their spouse’s name, with whites having the highest percentage of 86%. Additionally, I noticed that hispanic brides have the highest percentage of keeping their name with a percentage of 30% whereas white and black brides were less likely to keep their names. Also, black brides had the highest percentage amongst the three categories for hyphenated names at 16%. I wonder if culture and marital traditions play a big role in the differences between brides’ decisions with their last names across the three ethnicities/races. I also wonder what this data would have looked like a few decades ago and if the results would be significantly different from modern times. This relates to my community because I have witnessed all three options for last names occurring with married women, although taking their spouse’s name seems to be the most common, and it is important to recognize potential deeper meanings behind these choices. My headline for this graph would be: “Keeping vs. Changing Last Names - A Simple Concept with a Greater Meaning”.

raw_comment:
This graph depicts brides in opposite-sex marriages with their partner's last name. There are 3 options shown that depict what opposite-sex people do which are to take a spouse's name, keep their own last name, or hyphenate their last name with their partners. I noticed that the highest percentage of brides who took their husband's last names were white and the highest percentage of people who hyphenated their last names were black. I wonder how race affects this topic in the first place and why it's brought up -- like what does skin color have to do with marriage and taking your partner's last name? I think that the surveyors believe that race and ethnicity play a role due to the culture of that individual which can affect the decisions they make. This relates to my community because I firsthand know many women who have taken their husband's last names for personal life but would hyphenate them for business/job purposes. It depends on the individual and the choice that they make but personally, when the time comes to marry my future man I will take the traditional route and take his last name. 
Super Catchy Headline: "Who Cares Baby, I Think I Wanna Marry You"

raw_comment:
What I notice is that it is more common for white women to take their spouse's last name, whereas for Black women only 73% do and for Hispanic women, only 60% tend to take their spouse's last name. What I wonder is why more Black women seem to hyphenate their last name more than White and Hispanic women. Is it more of a traditional or cultural thing? Additionally, has the percentage of women keeping their last names gone up in the past 10-20 years since there have been changes in society regarding women and equal rights? What is going on in this graph is it is trying to show how the different races seem to differ quite greatly on the decision of a bride taking their spouses name or deciding to keep her own. Also, if they decide to hyphenate their last name as well. This relates to my community because I have an Aunt who decided to keep her original last name and when I was a kid I always wondered why she did that, so I would like to find out if there was a major underlying reason.

raw_comment:
I noticed that the majority of brides changed their last names in white, black, and Hispanic cultures. However, a lot of Hispanic Brides kept their last names. I wonder how tradition comes into the picture with this. Is it becoming more popular to keep last names? I would also wonder what other cultures, like Middle Eastern or Asian brides, would do with their last names. This relates to my community as I live in a predominantly white community and rarely see people keep their last name. This makes me wonder what I will do with my last name. 
I would title this: KEEP IT OR LEAVE IT

raw_comment:
I noticed that the highest percentages for all three groups changed their last name and took their spouse's last name. I also noticed that for whites and Hispanics more people kept their last name than hyphenating, but for blacks almost twice as many people hyphenated as those who kept their name. I wonder why more Hispanic people kept their last name than the other two races, and why more black people hyphenate than the other two. I also wonder how often these statistics change and what they will look like when I get married. This relates to me and my community because one day I will be a part of these groups and when I do get married I will have the choice of keeping my name, hyphenating, or going all the way to change my last name. 

My title is "Do you say 'I do' to a new last name?"

In the chart, I noticed that White women are most likely to take their spouse's last name with a 86% chance. This includes a 3% chance of White women who hyphenate their maiden and husband’s last name, and only a low 10% who actually keep their maiden name. On the other hand, Hispanic women are least likely to take their spouse's name with a 60% chance, and a 30% chance of keeping their maiden name. While Black women are most likely to hyphenate their last name. I wonder if it is most common for Hispanic women to keep their maiden name because of the importance of family. Also, Hispanic women often keep both their maiden name and add their husband’s last name on. Additionally, why are white women most likely to take their spouse’s name? This relates to my community as last names are a part of a person’s identity. When I get married, I will probably take my spouse’s last name, but I wonder how this will change for my friends.

raw_comment:
I notice that American women change their names to varying degrees: 86% of White brides, 73% of Black brides, 60% of Hispanic brides take their spouse's name. Interestingly, Black brides were most likely to hyphenate their names (16%) and Hispanic brides were more likely to keep their name (30%).

I wonder why such a large number of White brides take their spouse's name. Perhaps tradition dictates this trend. Furthermore, since Hispanic individuals often have more than one middle name, perhaps it is related to the bride's not changing their name. I wonder if fewer women will take their spouse's name in the future, considering how difficult it can be to change legal documents.

This relates to me and my community because my generation will be getting married in the next 15 years. As more couples are of mixed race, these statistics may change. I imagine that the number of brides that take their spouse's names will decrease across all races.

"Getting Hitched: Ditching the Name"

raw_comment:
This graph shows the amount of wives who took the last name of their spouse, based on race. The race with the highest rate of this is white, the race with the highest rate of keeping the last name is Hispanic, and the race with the highest rate of hyphenating the last name is Black. I wonder why this last phrase is true, because in my experience, I have seen Hispanic people combine their last name with their spouses. I also wonder how this information compares to the culture, traditions, and history of each race. This relates to me and my community because as society advances, I think that more and more wives will want to keep their last name and break stereotypical boundaries. I wonder how this graph will look in 20 years. 
"A Look At Last Name Trends Across Race"

raw_comment:
1) I notice that White brides are most likely to take their spouse's last names (86%), while Hispanic brides are least likely (60%). Hence, Hispanic brides (30%) are most likely to keep their last names. In the hyphenated category Black brides (16%) are also most likely to do so. 2) Why are Hispanic brides most likely to keep their last names? Is it tradition? What are the ages of these brides? May their opinion change based on age?

However, as the years pass and norms change there may be change for all as many more may want to stray from tradition.

raw_comment:
White brides tend to hold onto their names the least, with 86% choosing to take their spouses names. On the contrary, only 60% of Hispanic brides choose to take their spouse's name, with 30% keeping their surname. Black brides are in the middle, with 73% choosing to take their spouses names. They have the highest percentage (16%) of hyphenated names.

Why do white brides highly tend to take their spouses names while Hispanic brides don’t as much? Is this related to the differences between white and Hispanic cultures? It could possibly be due to gender dynamics between these cultures, though in the modern world these differences have been muted.

This shows the disparity between brides’ decisions to choose their surnames depending on their race. It isn’t of much impact to me, but it may be impactful to people who are dedicated to their surnames (like people who have important generational surnames).

Headline:
Identity in Marriage: Last Name Choices In Brides Reflect Cultural Diversity

raw_comment:
1. What do you notice? If your notice makes a claim, where in the graph is the evidence to support it?

Upon examining the graph, I noticed a trend where Hispanic women are more inclined to keep their own surnames rather than adopting their spouses'. In comparison to Hispanic women, White women exhibit a 26% lower likelihood of taking their spouse's last name. This distinction becomes significant when contrasting the naming decisions between Black and White women.

I'm curious about the absence of a total of 100% in the statistical percentages. Could there be an additional category completing the summaries? If not, does this impact the graph's credibility? It's essential for percentage statistics to sum up to 100%, so what implications does this variation hold for the graph?

This particular topic concerns both myself and my community, as many women in Andover have chosen to adopt their spouse's last name. However, my stepmother decided to retain her maiden name when she remarried.

raw_comment:
I notice that a higher percentage of white people are most often to change their last names. I also notice that Hispanics have the lowest percentage of changing their last names and have the highest percentage of keeping their last name. 

 I wonder what may be the reason for so many Hispanic brides to keep their own last names, whether it be a cultural reason or something else. And I also wonder why Black women tend to hyphenate their names more than any other race.

This relates to our community because some of us identify as one of those ethnicities and looking at this data encourages us to ask as to why we are seeing the trends we are seeing. It also helps us really know what our ethnicities values are. 

What If I Don't Want To Take My Spouses Name! It's More Common Than You Think.

1. The most noticeable statistic in the graph is that regardless of race, most brides take their spouses' last names. White brides tend to do this the most, and Hispanic brides tend to do this the least. However, a significant amount of Hispanic brides do keep their own last names.

2. I wonder what may be the reason for so many Hispanic brides to keep their own last names, whether it be a cultural reason or something else. And I also wonder why Black women tend to hyphenate their names more than any other race.

3. This graph is especially interesting to me because my mother is White and my father is Asian, yet my mother didn't take my dad's last name or even hyphenate it. While my mother kept her last name, my last name was the one that got hyphenated. My last name consists of my father's last name and then it's hyphenated to my mother's last name. So I don't even have the same last name as either of my parents, instead I have a union of them. 

4. If I were to retitle this graph, I would title it "What do brides do with their last names?"

I notice that White brides have the highest percentage of taking their spouse's name, followed closely by the percentage of Blacks that take their spouses last name. 
I wonder why Black brides are more likely to hyphenate their last name. I also wonder why Hispanic brides are the most likely to keep their last name. This makes me wonder if there is a cultural or religious aspect to it.

raw_comment:
What do you notice? - This graph shows whether a bride changed their last name, kept their last name, or hyphenated their last name. White woman make up the highest percentage of brides taking their spouses name at 86%, with black women following close behind with 73%. It's clear that in this survey, fewer women keep their name when they get married and even less hyphenate it. 
What do you wonder? - I wonder if taking a spouse's name has to do with someones culture, and if that is a confounding variable within the survey. 
How does this relate to you and your community? - My mom kept her last name, and it's interesting to see the information provided in this sample size. it demonstrates that women like my mom, infrequently keep their own name, which I think is very interesting. Most married women I know have taken their partners last name.

raw_comment:
What do you notice?
I notice that the majority of results from the graph show that regardless of race or ethnicity, most brides choose to change their last names. There is definitely more Hispanic people that choose to keep their name than white and black people, and there are hardly any people that made a hyphenated decision.
What do you wonder?
I wonder if the percentage of changing last names is so large due to religious beliefs and background of the husband or the wife. Many religions may require for the bride to take the husband's' last name when getting married. I also wonder why there are less people keeping their last name in the black community than in the white and hispanic community.
How does this relate to you and your community?
This impacts our community because through the process of getting married, all women have to choose what they want to do with their last name, and if they choose to change it they have to do a lot of complicated things along the way like, updating their insurance, or updating their bank account.

raw_comment:
What do you notice?
I notice that the majority of results from the graph show that regardless of race or ethnicity, most brides choose to change their last names. There is definitely more Hispanic people that choose to keep their name than white and black people, and there are hardly any people that made a hyphenated decision.
What do you wonder?
I wonder if the percentage of changing last names is so large due to religious beliefs and background of the husband or the wife. Many religions may require for the bride to take the husband's' last name when getting married. I also wonder why there are less people keeping their last name in the black community than in the white and hispanic community.
How does this relate to you and your community?
This impacts our community because through the process of getting married, all women have to choose what they want to do with their last name, and if they choose to change it they have to do a lot of complicated things along the way like, updating their insurance, or updating their bank account.

1. What do you notice? If your notice makes a claim, where in the graph is the evidence to support it?

Different communities, different choices, different names.

"NAME CHANGE"

I notice the percentages don't add up to 100, they add up to either 98 or 99. The graph implies that brides who are white more often take their spouses names. This impacts me and my community because women often submit to the most common custom - to take their husbands last name. If I marry, I will have to face this choice, and seeing this graph can affect that choice.

raw_comment:
1. I notice that the majority of women choose to take their spouse's name, with this being most common for white women. Hispanic women were the most varied and most likely to keep their last name out of the three demographics. Also, the percentages don't add up to 100, probably because the percentages were rounded.
2. I wonder what a graph that showed this data over time, by age, or by state would look like. I also wonder what insight we would gain if we looked at this data next to what men do with their last names (probably very few would do anything other than keep it), or if we asked the people what went into their decision.
3. This affects me, because as a girl/woman, this decision about what to do with your last name when you get married seems sort of symbolic, and it's also not something people talk about very often.
4. Brides Around the Country Still Subscribing to Traditional Marriage Custom

raw_comment: I find it weird how each race has a higher chance of doing different things with their last name. Like, White people have almost a 90% chance to change their name, meanwhile Black and Hispanic people only have 60-70%. Hispanic people almost have a 1 out of 3 chance of not changing their name, which could be because of cultural practices, but the White people and Black people only have around a 10% chance. And finally, Black people have around a 15% chance to hyphenate their last name, compared to 3% and 9%. These large differences from one race and the others could be because of cultural appropriation of these different races, but it also could be societal norms. Contradicting this, though, all races have an extremely high chance to change their last name, and I wonder why they all have such a high chance to. I feel like it could be because of how society has made this the default way of name-changing to change your last name to your significant others' last name, probably to show your love and commitment in this relationship, but then again, there is no definite answer.
